**The Quiet Chaos of Being Alive**

There’s a strange, almost electric hum to existence that I can’t quite name. It’s not the kind of thing you notice when you’re busy—when you’re scrolling through your phone, when you’re rushing to work, when you’re pretending to listen to someone talk while your mind drifts to the laundry you forgot to fold. But when you slow down, when the world quiets just enough for you to hear the blood in your veins, that hum is there. It’s the sound of being alive, of being a body that breathes and a mind that wanders and a heart that, against all odds, keeps beating even when you forget to feed it.

I’ve been thinking a lot about time lately—not in the abstract, philosophical way, but in the way it gnaws at the edges of everything. How it stretches and compresses without warning. How a single moment can feel like an eternity when you’re waiting for a text back, and how years can vanish in the blink of an eye when you’re not paying attention. I turned 30 recently, and instead of the grand revelations I expected—some deep, life-altering epiphany—I just felt… older. Not in the way that makes you feel wise or accomplished, but in the way that makes you realize you’ve been alive for three decades and still don’t know what you’re doing half the time.

There’s a comfort in that, though. The not-knowing. The way life is less a straight line and more a series of detours, some scenic, some pothole-ridden, all of them necessary. I used to think I was supposed to have it all figured out by now. That by 30, I’d have a career that made sense, a relationship that stuck, a home that felt permanent, a sense of self that wasn’t constantly shifting like sand. But now I see that the figuring-out is the point. The detours are the map.

I’ve been reading a lot of poetry lately—mostly because I need something that doesn’t require me to solve anything, just to sit with the words and let them do their work. There’s a line from Mary Oliver that’s been stuck in my head: *"Tell me, what is it you plan to do with your one wild and precious life?"* It’s the kind of question that sounds profound until you realize it’s not actually asking for an answer. It’s just reminding you that your life is wild and precious, whether you’re living it right or not. Whether you’re making the most of it or wasting it in front of a Netflix show at 2 AM. Whether you’re happy or miserable or somewhere in between. It’s still yours. Still *yours*.

I wonder sometimes if the reason we’re all so obsessed with productivity, with hustle culture, with the idea that we have to be *doing* something meaningful all the time, is because we’re afraid of the quiet. Afraid of the moments when we’re not achieving, not consuming, not performing. Afraid of the hum of existence that doesn’t come with a to-do list. But what if the hum is the point? What if the chaos of being alive—the way your thoughts spiral, the way your body aches in the morning, the way love and loss and boredom and joy all live in the same chest—isn’t something to escape, but something to witness?

I’ve been writing this for a while now, and I still don’t know what it’s *about*. Maybe it’s not supposed to be about anything. Maybe it’s just a record of a few minutes in the life of someone who’s trying to pay attention. Trying to notice the way the light hits the wall in the afternoon, the way a stranger’s laugh sounds like a secret, the way grief and gratitude can live in the same breath. Maybe the point isn’t to have answers, but to keep asking questions. To keep letting the hum of life vibrate through you, even when it’s uncomfortable.

There’s a tree outside my window that I’ve watched change with the seasons. In the winter, it’s just bare branches against the gray sky. In the spring, it’s a riot of green. In the fall, it’s a slow burn of gold before it lets go. And every time I look at it, I think about how much it resembles being human. How we, too, are just trying to hold on to something beautiful while the world changes around us. How we, too, are temporary. How we, too, are alive.

So here’s to the quiet chaos. To the not-knowing. To the hum. To the moments when you forget to be impressive and just *are*. That’s enough. More than enough.
